claim: Endocannabinoids are recently recognized regulators of brain development.
source: Endocannabinoids are recently recognized regulators of brain development, but molecular effectors downstream of type-1 cannabinoid receptor (CB1R)-activation remain incompletely understood.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader scientific literature context provided in the manuscript.

claim: Molecular effectors downstream of CB1R-activation remain incompletely understood.
source: Endocannabinoids are recently recognized regulators of brain development, but molecular effectors downstream of type-1 cannabinoid receptor (CB1R)-activation remain incompletely understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Neuronal CB1Rs couple to heterotrimeric G12/G13 proteins after activation by endo- or exocannabinoids.
source: We report atypical coupling of neuronal CB1Rs, after activation by endo- or exocannabinoids such as the marijuana component ∆9-tetrahydrocannabinol, to heterotrimeric G12/G13 proteins that triggers rapid and reversible non-muscle myosin II (NM II) dependent contraction of the actomyosin cytoskeleton, through a Rho-GTPase and Rho-associated kinase (ROCK).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CB1R activation by cannabinoids triggers rapid and reversible NM II-dependent contraction of the actomyosin cytoskeleton.
source: We report atypical coupling of neuronal CB1Rs, after activation by endo- or exocannabinoids such as the marijuana component ∆9-tetrahydrocannabinol, to heterotrimeric G12/G13 proteins that triggers rapid and reversible non-muscle myosin II (NM II) dependent contraction of the actomyosin cytoskeleton, through a Rho-GTPase and Rho-associated kinase (ROCK).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing blebbistatin (NM II inhibitor) blocks cannabinoid-induced effects (Figures 2, 3).

claim: CB1R-induced actomyosin contraction occurs through Rho-GTPase and ROCK.
source: We report atypical coupling of neuronal CB1Rs, after activation by endo- or exocannabinoids such as the marijuana component ∆9-tetrahydrocannabinol, to heterotrimeric G12/G13 proteins that triggers rapid and reversible non-muscle myosin II (NM II) dependent contraction of the actomyosin cytoskeleton, through a Rho-GTPase and Rho-associated kinase (ROCK).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments with C3 transferase (Rho inhibitor) and Y-27632 (ROCK inhibitor) shown in Figure 3.

claim: CB1R activation induces rapid neuronal remodeling including retraction of neurites and axonal growth cones.
source: This induces rapid neuronal remodeling, such as retraction of neurites and axonal growth cones, elevated neuronal rigidity, and reshaping of somatodendritic morphology.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse microscopy data in Figures 1, 4, 6, and 7.

claim: CB1R activation elevates neuronal rigidity.
source: This induces rapid neuronal remodeling, such as retraction of neurites and axonal growth cones, elevated neuronal rigidity, and reshaping of somatodendritic morphology.
evidence: This is supported by atomic force microscopy measurements shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: CB1R activation reshapes somatodendritic morphology.
source: This induces rapid neuronal remodeling, such as retraction of neurites and axonal growth cones, elevated neuronal rigidity, and reshaping of somatodendritic morphology.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 7.

claim: Chronic pharmacological inhibition of NM II prevents cannabinoid-induced reduction of dendritic development in vitro.
source: Chronic pharmacological inhibition of NM II prevents cannabinoid-induced reduction of dendritic development in vitro and leads, similarly to blockade of endocannabinoid action, to excessive growth of corticofugal axons into the sub-ventricular zone in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7B-C showing blebbistatin treatment prevents WIN-induced reduction in dendrite number.

claim: Chronic pharmacological inhibition of NM II leads to excessive growth of corticofugal axons into the sub-ventricular zone in vivo.
source: Chronic pharmacological inhibition of NM II prevents cannabinoid-induced reduction of dendritic development in vitro and leads, similarly to blockade of endocannabinoid action, to excessive growth of corticofugal axons into the sub-ventricular zone in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero injection experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Blockade of endocannabinoid action leads to excessive growth of corticofugal axons into the sub-ventricular zone in vivo.
source: Chronic pharmacological inhibition of NM II prevents cannabinoid-induced reduction of dendritic development in vitro and leads, similarly to blockade of endocannabinoid action, to excessive growth of corticofugal axons into the sub-ventricular zone in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experiments with CB1R antagonist AM251 shown in Figure 5E, E', G.

claim: CB1R can rapidly transform the neuronal cytoskeleton through actomyosin contractility.
source: Our results suggest that CB1R can rapidly transform the neuronal cytoskeleton through actomyosin contractility, resulting in cellular remodeling events ultimately able to affect the brain architecture and wiring.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: CB1R-induced actomyosin contractility results in cellular remodeling events able to affect brain architecture and wiring.
source: Our results suggest that CB1R can rapidly transform the neuronal cytoskeleton through actomyosin contractility, resulting in cellular remodeling events ultimately able to affect the brain architecture and wiring.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion linking the cellular-level findings to broader developmental outcomes, supported by in vivo data in Figure 5.

claim: The endocannabinoid system is an important regulator of brain wiring during development.
source: The endocannabinoid (eCB) system is emerging as an important regulator of brain wiring during development with a variety of functions, ranging from lineage segregation of stem cells to refinement of synaptic functions in complex neuronal networks (Williams et al., 2003; Berghuis et al., 2007; Harkany et al., 2008; Mulder et al., 2008; Vitalis et al., 2008; Watson et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Endocannabinoid functions range from lineage segregation of stem cells to refinement of synaptic functions.
source: The endocannabinoid (eCB) system is emerging as an important regulator of brain wiring during development with a variety of functions, ranging from lineage segregation of stem cells to refinement of synaptic functions in complex neuronal networks (Williams et al., 2003; Berghuis et al., 2007; Harkany et al., 2008; Mulder et al., 2008; Vitalis et al., 2008; Watson et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: In both embryonic and adult brains, endocannabinoid action is predominantly mediated by CB1 cannabinoid receptors.
source: In both the embryonic and adult brains, eCB action is predominantly mediated by CB1 cannabinoid receptors (CB1Rs), which is one of the most highly expressed neuronal G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), known to couple to Gi/o heterotrimeric proteins (Howlett, 2005), but the molecular mechanisms by which CB1R shapes developing neurons remain mostly unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Howlett, 2005.

claim: CB1R is one of the most highly expressed neuronal G-protein-coupled receptors.
source: In both the embryonic and adult brains, eCB action is predominantly mediated by CB1 cannabinoid receptors (CB1Rs), which is one of the most highly expressed neuronal G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), known to couple to Gi/o heterotrimeric proteins (Howlett, 2005), but the molecular mechanisms by which CB1R shapes developing neurons remain mostly unknown.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: CB1Rs are known to couple to Gi/o heterotrimeric proteins.
source: In both the embryonic and adult brains, eCB action is predominantly mediated by CB1 cannabinoid receptors (CB1Rs), which is one of the most highly expressed neuronal G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), known to couple to Gi/o heterotrimeric proteins (Howlett, 2005), but the molecular mechanisms by which CB1R shapes developing neurons remain mostly unknown.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Howlett, 2005.

claim: The molecular mechanisms by which CB1R shapes developing neurons remain mostly unknown.
source: In both the embryonic and adult brains, eCB action is predominantly mediated by CB1 cannabinoid receptors (CB1Rs), which is one of the most highly expressed neuronal G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), known to couple to Gi/o heterotrimeric proteins (Howlett, 2005), but the molecular mechanisms by which CB1R shapes developing neurons remain mostly unknown.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claim: The exact role of endocannabinoids in shaping neuronal architecture is under debate.
source: The exact role of eCBs in shaping the neuronal architecture is also under debate, since several reports indicate neurite retraction, while others found the induction of neurite outgrowth following CB1R activation (review in Gaffuri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article discussing conflicting findings.

claim: Several reports indicate neurite retraction following CB1R activation.
source: The exact role of eCBs in shaping the neuronal architecture is also under debate, since several reports indicate neurite retraction, while others found the induction of neurite outgrowth following CB1R activation (review in Gaffuri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Some reports found induction of neurite outgrowth following CB1R activation.
source: The exact role of eCBs in shaping the neuronal architecture is also under debate, since several reports indicate neurite retraction, while others found the induction of neurite outgrowth following CB1R activation (review in Gaffuri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Endocannabinoids have locally repulsive effects at axonal growth cones.
source: Likewise, currently it is difficult to reconcile the locally repulsive effects of eCBs, reported at axonal growth cones (Berghuis et al., 2007; Argaw et al., 2011), and their role of mediating efficient directional axonal growth and shaping well-fasciculated axonal tracts (Mulder et al., 2008; Vitalis et al., 2008; Watson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berghuis et al., 2007 and Argaw et al., 2011.

claim: Endocannabinoids mediate efficient directional axonal growth and shape well-fasciculated axonal tracts.
source: Likewise, currently it is difficult to reconcile the locally repulsive effects of eCBs, reported at axonal growth cones (Berghuis et al., 2007; Argaw et al., 2011), and their role of mediating efficient directional axonal growth and shaping well-fasciculated axonal tracts (Mulder et al., 2008; Vitalis et al., 2008; Watson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The neuronal cytoskeleton is composed of filamentous-actin and microtubule networks.
source: This structure is stabilized by the cytoskeleton, which, similar to non-neuronal cells, is composed of two major polymers, the highly plastic filamentous-actin (F-actin) and the more stable microtubule (MT) networks.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: Actin filaments are often cross-linked to non-muscle myosin II.
source: Actin filaments are often cross-linked to a molecular motor protein, the non-muscle myosin II (NM II), whose contractile properties further endow the actomyosin network with highly dynamic control of cell behavior and architecture (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Non-muscle myosin II's contractile properties endow the actomyosin network with dynamic control of cell behavior and architecture.
source: Actin filaments are often cross-linked to a molecular motor protein, the non-muscle myosin II (NM II), whose contractile properties further endow the actomyosin network with highly dynamic control of cell behavior and architecture (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009.

claim: The cytoskeleton is mainly regulated by Rho-like GTPases.
source: The cytoskeleton is mainly regulated by Rho-like GTPases that control a wide variety of effector mechanisms such as actin polymerization and branching, actomyosin contractility, focal adhesions, microtubule dynamics, and membrane transport (Kaibuchi et al., 1999; Etienne-Manneville and Hall, 2002; Hall and Lalli, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rho-like GTPases control actin polymerization and branching, actomyosin contractility, focal adhesions, microtubule dynamics, and membrane transport.
source: The cytoskeleton is mainly regulated by Rho-like GTPases that control a wide variety of effector mechanisms such as actin polymerization and branching, actomyosin contractility, focal adhesions, microtubule dynamics, and membrane transport (Kaibuchi et al., 1999; Etienne-Manneville and Hall, 2002; Hall and Lalli, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: ROCK is a key activator protein of convergent signaling pathways downstream of Rho-GTPases.
source: Downstream protein kinases such as the Rho-associated, coiled coil-containing kinase (ROCK) are the key activator proteins of these convergent-signaling pathways.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell signaling.

claim: ROCK is associated with particular CB1R-induced phenotypes.
source: Interestingly, ROCK is associated with particular CB1R-induced phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies described in the following sentences.

claim: In CB1R-over-expressing B103 cells, anandamide induces cell rounding via ROCK.
source: In CB1R-over-expressing B103 cells, the endocannabinoid anandamide induces cell rounding via ROCK (Ishii and Chun, 2002), and CB1R activation results in RhoA- and ROCK-dependent repulsion of growth cones of cultured hippocampal neurons (Berghuis et al., 2007), but neither the coupling mechanism of CB1R to ROCK nor the cytoskeletal targets downstream of CB1R-activated ROCK are identified yet.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ishii and Chun, 2002.

claim: CB1R activation results in RhoA- and ROCK-dependent repulsion of growth cones of cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: In CB1R-over-expressing B103 cells, the endocannabinoid anandamide induces cell rounding via ROCK (Ishii and Chun, 2002), and CB1R activation results in RhoA- and ROCK-dependent repulsion of growth cones of cultured hippocampal neurons (Berghuis et al., 2007), but neither the coupling mechanism of CB1R to ROCK nor the cytoskeletal targets downstream of CB1R-activated ROCK are identified yet.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berghuis et al., 2007.

claim: The coupling mechanism of CB1R to ROCK is not yet identified.
source: In CB1R-over-expressing B103 cells, the endocannabinoid anandamide induces cell rounding via ROCK (Ishii and Chun, 2002), and CB1R activation results in RhoA- and ROCK-dependent repulsion of growth cones of cultured hippocampal neurons (Berghuis et al., 2007), but neither the coupling mechanism of CB1R to ROCK nor the cytoskeletal targets downstream of CB1R-activated ROCK are identified yet.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The cytoskeletal targets downstream of CB1R-activated ROCK are not yet identified.
source: In CB1R-over-expressing B103 cells, the endocannabinoid anandamide induces cell rounding via ROCK (Ishii and Chun, 2002), and CB1R activation results in RhoA- and ROCK-dependent repulsion of growth cones of cultured hippocampal neurons (Berghuis et al., 2007), but neither the coupling mechanism of CB1R to ROCK nor the cytoskeletal targets downstream of CB1R-activated ROCK are identified yet.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: LifeAct allows observation of the dynamic actin network without perturbing natural reorganization kinetics.
source: This actin-binding peptide allows observation of the dynamic actin network without perturbing natural reorganization kinetics (Riedl et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riedl et al., 2008.

claim: Cultured hippocampal neurons expressing Flag-CB1R-eGFP and LifeAct-mCherry show F-actin-rich dynamic growth cones.
source: Time-lapse microscopy of live neurons, expressing Flag-CB1R-eGFP and LifeAct-mCherry, showed numerous F-actin-rich dynamic growth cones (Figure 1A) advancing at individually variable velocities (Figure 1A,B), but yielding a fairly constant mean growth rate of 20–30 µm/hr (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Growth cones advance at a mean growth rate of 20-30 µm/hr.
source: Time-lapse microscopy of live neurons, expressing Flag-CB1R-eGFP and LifeAct-mCherry, showed numerous F-actin-rich dynamic growth cones (Figure 1A) advancing at individually variable velocities (Figure 1A,B), but yielding a fairly constant mean growth rate of 20–30 µm/hr (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Bath application of 100 nM WIN 55,212-2 leads to rapid retraction of the F-actin-rich domain.
source: Strikingly, bath application of 100 nM WIN 55,212-2 (WIN), a synthetic cannabinoid agonist, led to a rapid retraction of the F-actin-rich domain (Figure 1A), with mean retraction amplitude of 62.2 µm ± 5.2 (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse microscopy data in Figure 1A, C-E.

claim: WIN-induced retraction has a mean amplitude of 62.2 µm ± 5.2.
source: Strikingly, bath application of 100 nM WIN 55,212-2 (WIN), a synthetic cannabinoid agonist, led to a rapid retraction of the F-actin-rich domain (Figure 1A), with mean retraction amplitude of 62.2 µm ± 5.2 (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: WIN-induced retraction is detectable at 2 min after agonist exposure.
source: Retraction was already detectable at 2 min after agonist exposure and typically reached a plateau between 10 and 20 min (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course data in Figure 1C, D.

claim: WIN-induced retraction typically reaches a plateau between 10 and 20 min.
source: Retraction was already detectable at 2 min after agonist exposure and typically reached a plateau between 10 and 20 min (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course data in Figure 1C, D.

claim: Retracted axons are characterized by an F-actin-rich retraction bulb and a thin membranous trailing remnant.
source: The morphology of retracted axons was characterized by an F-actin-rich retraction bulb (arrowheads on Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and a thin membranous trailing remnant (open arrowheads on Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), the latter of which was not included in the length measurement.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy images in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pre-treatment with CB1R antagonist AM281 (1 µM) inhibits WIN-induced retraction.
source: Pre-treatment with the CB1R selective antagonist/inverse agonist AM281 (AM) (1 µM) inhibited retraction (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1D, E.

claim: 2-arachidonoylglycerol (1 µM) produces significant growth cone retraction.
source: Further pharmacological characterization showed that several other chemically distinct CB1R agonists, the endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) (1 µM), the principal psychoactive marijuana constituent Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9-THC) (1 µM) and the synthetic agonists CP55,940 (100 nM) and HU-210 (100 nM) also produced significant retraction (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1E.

claim: Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (1 µM) produces significant growth cone retraction.
source: Further pharmacological characterization showed that several other chemically distinct CB1R agonists, the endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) (1 µM), the principal psychoactive marijuana constituent Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9-THC) (1 µM) and the synthetic agonists CP55,940 (100 nM) and HU-210 (100 nM) also produced significant retraction (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1E.

claim: CP55,940 (100 nM) produces significant growth cone retraction.
source: Further pharmacological characterization showed that several other chemically distinct CB1R agonists, the endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) (1 µM), the principal psychoactive marijuana constituent Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9-THC) (1 µM) and the synthetic agonists CP55,940 (100 nM) and HU-210 (100 nM) also produced significant retraction (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1E.

claim: HU-210 (100 nM) produces significant growth cone retraction.
source: Further pharmacological characterization showed that several other chemically distinct CB1R agonists, the endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) (1 µM), the principal psychoactive marijuana constituent Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9-THC) (1 µM) and the synthetic agonists CP55,940 (100 nM) and HU-210 (100 nM) also produced significant retraction (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1E.

claim: WIN-induced retraction is saturable and concentration-dependent with an EC50 of around 20 nM.
source: The retraction was saturable and concentration-dependent with a half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) value of around 20 nM for WIN (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response curve data in Figure 1F.

claim: Cannabinoid-induced growth cone retraction is reversible after ligand wash-out.
source: When treatment with 25 nM WIN was followed by ligand-free wash-out, growth cone progression resumed normally showing the reversibility of cannabinoid-induced growth cone retraction (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by wash-out experiment data in Figure 1G.

claim: WIN-induced retraction occurs in neurons expressing only endogenous CB1Rs.
source: Finally, this retraction was not a result of CB1R over-expression since treatment with 100 nM WIN or 1 µM 2-AG induced significant retraction with similar kinetics in neurons transfected only with LifeAct-mCherry (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in neurons not overexpressing CB1R, shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: The mean amplitude of retraction is lower in neurons expressing endogenous CB1Rs compared to those overexpressing CB1Rs.
source: However, the mean amplitude of retraction was lower and responses were more variable than in Flag-CB1R-eGFP-expressing neurons (compare Figure 1C,D with Figure 1H,I), as expected in a heterogeneous neuronal population expressing endogenous CB1Rs at highly variable levels (Leterrier et al., 2006).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing data in Figure 1C, D with Figure 1H, I.

claim: Growth cone advance rapidly resumes even in the continued presence of 100 nM WIN in neurons expressing endogenous CB1Rs.
source: In addition, growth cone advance rapidly resumed even in the continued presence of 100 nM WIN (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course data in Figure 1H.

claim: F-actin redistributes from growth cones into a cable-like pattern on the distal axonal shaft within 2-4 min after WIN stimulation.
source: A significant portion of F-actin redistributed in the first 2–4 min after stimulation from its original location in growth cones into a more homogenous cable-like pattern on the distal axonal shaft (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microtubules bend and form periodic local loops within 2-4 min after WIN stimulation.
source: In contrast, MTs bent during the same time frame forming periodic local loops (Figure 2A,A',B and Video 1) before finally consolidating into a homogenously labeled retraction bulb.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 2A, A', B and Video 1.

claim: F-actin cables often co-localize with regions displaying periodic bends in microtubules.
source: The F-actin cables (bundles of F-actin filaments, which are not separately resolved here by diffraction-limited microscopy), often co-localized with regions displaying periodic bends in MTs (Figure 2B'), suggesting that an F-actin-related force pulls strongly enough to bend MTs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-localization imaging in Figure 2B'.

claim: An F-actin-related force pulls strongly enough to bend microtubules.
source: The F-actin cables (bundles of F-actin filaments, which are not separately resolved here by diffraction-limited microscopy), often co-localized with regions displaying periodic bends in MTs (Figure 2B'), suggesting that an F-actin-related force pulls strongly enough to bend MTs.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization of F-actin cables with MT bends shown in Figure 2B'.

claim: Periodic MT bends occur in neurons not expressing cytoskeletal markers EB3-eGFP or LifeAct-mCherry.
source: This effect was not the result of the over-expression of the cytoskeletal markers EB3-eGFP or LifeAct-mCherry, since we could observe similar periodic MT bends, detected by post hoc immunohistochemistry, in neurons not expressing these markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nocodazole pre-treatment stops growth cone advance but WIN still induces significant retraction.
source: Nocodazole pre-treatment stopped growth cone advance but WIN still induced significant retraction (Figure 2C,D, Figure 3E and Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2C, D, Figure 3E and Video 2.

claim: Cytochalasin D inhibits both growth cone advance and WIN-induced retraction.
source: In contrast, cytochalasin D inhibited both growth cone advance and WIN-induced retraction (Figure 2E,F, Figure 3E and Video 3) showing that while the presence of both F-actin and MTs is necessary for growth cone advance, as reported previously (Dent et al., 2003), only F-actin is necessary for CB1R-induced retraction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2E, F, Figure 3E and Video 3.

claim: Both F-actin and microtubules are necessary for growth cone advance.
source: In contrast, cytochalasin D inhibited both growth cone advance and WIN-induced retraction (Figure 2E,F, Figure 3E and Video 3) showing that while the presence of both F-actin and MTs is necessary for growth cone advance, as reported previously (Dent et al., 2003), only F-actin is necessary for CB1R-induced retraction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Dent et al., 2003.

claim: Only F-actin is necessary for CB1R-induced retraction.
source: In contrast, cytochalasin D inhibited both growth cone advance and WIN-induced retraction (Figure 2E,F, Figure 3E and Video 3) showing that while the presence of both F-actin and MTs is necessary for growth cone advance, as reported previously (Dent et al., 2003), only F-actin is necessary for CB1R-induced retraction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing effects of nocodazole (which doesn't block retraction) and cytochalasin D (which does block retraction) in Figure 2 and 3.

claim: WIN treatment induces rapid and strong upregulation of myosin light chain phosphorylation in the distal axon adjacent to the F-actin-rich growth cone at 2 min.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis of WIN-treated F-actin-rich growth cones at 2 min after the addition of WIN strikingly showed rapid and strong up-regulation of myosin light chain phosphorylation in the distal axon, adjacent to the F-actin-rich growth cone (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), at the right place for the subsequent NMII-dependent contraction, both in neurons transfected only with LifeAct-mCherry (Figure 3A–C) and with Flag-CB1R-eCFP and LifeAct-mCherry (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blebbistatin pre-treatment completely abolishes WIN-mediated retraction.
source: Remarkably, blebbistatin completely abolished WIN-mediated retraction of these dynamically advancing F-actin-rich structures (Figure 2G,H, Figure 3E and Video 4), suggesting that the main force-generating factor downstream of CB1R activation is actomyosin contractility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2G, H, Figure 3E and Video 4.

claim: The main force-generating factor downstream of CB1R activation is actomyosin contractility.
source: Remarkably, blebbistatin completely abolished WIN-mediated retraction of these dynamically advancing F-actin-rich structures (Figure 2G,H, Figure 3E and Video 4), suggesting that the main force-generating factor downstream of CB1R activation is actomyosin contractility.
evidence: This is inferred from the complete blockade of retraction by blebbistatin, a specific NM II inhibitor.

claim: The inhibitory effect of blebbistatin on WIN-induced retraction is concentration dependent with EC50 of 116 nM.
source: This inhibitory effect of blebbistatin was concentration dependent with half-maximal value of inhibition (EC50) of 116 nM (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment induces transformation of growth cone lamellipodia into several dynamically advancing filopodia.
source: Blebbistatin pre-treatment induced substantial morphological changes of the growth cone, which continued to move forward in a rather disorganized fashion (Figure 2G and Video 4), typically transforming the growth cone lamellipodia into several dynamically advancing filopodia, as reported previously (Rosner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2G and Video 4, and supported by citation to Rosner et al., 2007.

claim: Treatment with blebbistatin or ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 significantly inhibits endogenous CB1R-induced retraction of growth cones.
source: First, we showed that NMII-dependent growth cone contraction is not a result of CB1R over-expression, since treatment with blebbistatin (25 µM) or the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (10 µM) (Figure 3D) significantly inhibited endogenous CB1R-induced retraction of growth cones, previously presented on Figure 1I, in neurons transfected only with LifeAct-mCherry and EB3-eGFP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3D.

claim: Pre-treatment with Rho inhibitor C3 transferase significantly reduces WIN-mediated retraction amplitude.
source: The amplitude of WIN-mediated retraction was significantly reduced by pre-treatment with the Rho inhibitor C3 transferase (1 µg/ml, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (10 µM) (Figure 3E), but not by the MLCK-specific inhibitor ML-7 (30 µM) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pre-treatment with ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 significantly reduces WIN-mediated retraction amplitude.
source: The amplitude of WIN-mediated retraction was significantly reduced by pre-treatment with the Rho inhibitor C3 transferase (1 µg/ml, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (10 µM) (Figure 3E), but not by the MLCK-specific inhibitor ML-7 (30 µM) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3E.

claim: MLCK-specific inhibitor ML-7 does not significantly reduce WIN-mediated retraction amplitude.
source: The amplitude of WIN-mediated retraction was significantly reduced by pre-treatment with the Rho inhibitor C3 transferase (1 µg/ml, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (10 µM) (Figure 3E), but not by the MLCK-specific inhibitor ML-7 (30 µM) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3E.

claim: Treatment with inactive (R)-(+)-blebbistatin stereoisomer is ineffective at blocking WIN-induced retraction.
source: Treatment with the inactive (R)-(+)-blebbistatin (25 µM) stereoisomer was ineffective (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text as a control experiment.

claim: siRNA knock-down of endogenous NM IIA and NM IIB results in significant reduction of WIN-mediated contractility.
source: The implication of neuronal NM II was further confirmed by siRNA knock-down of endogenous NM IIA and NM IIB (Miserey-Lenkei et al., 2010), which resulted in significant reduction of WIN-mediated contractility as compared to control (anti-luciferase) siRNA (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiments in Figure 3F.

claim: Treatment with pertussis toxin does not significantly decrease cannabinoid-induced growth cone retraction.
source: Notably, treatment with pertussis toxin (100 ng/µl), a specific inhibitor of Gi/o heterotrimeric proteins, which are generally considered as the main signaling pathway of CB1Rs (Howlett, 2005), did not decrease significantly cannabinoid-induced growth cone retraction (Figure 3E), similarly to a previously reported finding for ROCK-mediated induced cell rounding after anandamide treatment (Ishii and Chun, 2002).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3E.

claim: G12/G13 proteins may mediate rapid growth cone collapse, neurite retraction, and cell rounding in neuronal cell lines in response to certain GPCR agonists.
source: Another family of heterotrimeric G-proteins, G12/G13, may mediate rapid growth cone collapse, neurite retraction, and cell rounding in neuronal cell lines in response to certain GPCR agonists such as lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) (Katoh et al., 1998; Kranenburg et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Katoh et al., 1998 and Kranenburg et al., 1999.

claim: Combined siRNA knockdown of G12 and G13 efficiently inhibits WIN-mediated contractility.
source: However, when we combined together 2 siRNAs of each pool, each resulting mixed pools efficiently inhibited WIN-mediated contractility (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiments in Figure 3F.

claim: The presence of either G12 or G13 is necessary and sufficient for CB1R-induced actomyosin contraction.
source: These results show that the presence of either G12 or G13 is necessary and sufficient for CB1R-induced actomyosin contraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the siRNA knockdown experiments showing that both G12 and G13 must be knocked down to block the effect.

claim: Application of 1 µM WIN results in significant retraction of corticofugal growth cones in organotypic slices.
source: In organotypic slices prepared from the offspring between postnatal day 4 and 6 (P4–P6), numerous corticofugal F-actin-rich growth cones from layer II–III pyramidal neurons could be visualized by video microscopy at 48 hr after slice preparation (Figure 4A). Application of 1 µM WIN resulted in significant retraction of growth cones (Figure 4B,D and Video 5) through activation of CB1R since this effect could be prevented by pre-treatment with 5 µM AM281 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging data in organotypic slices shown in Figure 4B, D and Video 5.

claim: Pre-treatment with 5 µM AM281 prevents WIN-induced retraction in organotypic slices.
source: Application of 1 µM WIN resulted in significant retraction of growth cones (Figure 4B,D and Video 5) through activation of CB1R since this effect could be prevented by pre-treatment with 5 µM AM281 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4D.

claim: WIN-induced retraction displays slower kinetics ex vivo than in vitro.
source: This retraction displayed slower kinetics ex vivo than in vitro (compare to Figure 1) probably due to limited diffusion of the highly hydrophobic WIN into the slice and/or into differences in adhesive and mechanistic properties within the organotypic brain slice.
evidence: This is observed by comparing time-course data in Figure 4 with Figure 1.

claim: WIN-mediated activation of endogenous CB1Rs leads to arrest or retraction of growth cones in organotypic slices.
source: WIN-mediated activation of endogenous CB1Rs typically led to arrest or retraction of numerous growth cones (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in neurons expressing only cytoskeletal markers in Figure 4C, E.

claim: Pre-treatment with blebbistatin efficiently blocks WIN-induced growth cone arrest or retraction in organotypic slices.
source: Importantly, pre-treatment with blebbistatin (25 µM) efficiently blocked this effect (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4E.

claim: 100% of blebbistatin-injected embryos survived and developed without apparent gross anatomical brain defects.
source: Notably, 100% of blebbistatin-injected embryos survived and developed without apparent gross anatomical brain defects, suggesting that neuronal NM II can be safely targeted in vivo.
evidence: This is an observation from the in vivo injection experiments.

claim: In embryos treated with active (S)-(−)-blebbistatin between E15 and E17, Tuj1-expressing axons show important targeting errors by invading the sub-ventricular zone.
source: In embryos treated between E15 and E17 with active (S)-(−)-blebbistatin (Figure 5D,D´,G), but not with the inactive (R)-(+) stereoisomer (Figure 5C,C´,G), Tuj1-expressing axons showed important targeting errors, by invading the sub-ventricular zone, from which CB1R-expressing corticofugal axons are usually excluded (Figure 5B,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo injection experiments and histological analysis in Figure 5D, D', G.

claim: Treatment with inactive (R)-(+) blebbistatin stereoisomer does not cause axonal targeting errors.
source: In embryos treated between E15 and E17 with active (S)-(−)-blebbistatin (Figure 5D,D´,G), but not with the inactive (R)-(+) stereoisomer (Figure 5C,C´,G), Tuj1-expressing axons showed important targeting errors, by invading the sub-ventricular zone, from which CB1R-expressing corticofugal axons are usually excluded (Figure 5B,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo injection experiments in Figure 5C, C', G.

claim: CB1R-expressing corticofugal axons are usually excluded from the sub-ventricular zone.
source: In embryos treated between E15 and E17 with active (S)-(−)-blebbistatin (Figure 5D,D´,G), but not with the inactive (R)-(+) stereoisomer (Figure 5C,C´,G), Tuj1-expressing axons showed important targeting errors, by invading the sub-ventricular zone, from which CB1R-expressing corticofugal axons are usually excluded (Figure 5B,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control histological data in Figure 5B.

claim: Treatment with CB1R antagonist AM251 leads to similar developmental phenotype as blebbistatin treatment.
source: Treatment with the CB1R-specific antagonist AM251 (1 mM) but not with its vehicle (DMSO 2.8%) led to similar developmental phenotype (Figure 5E,E´,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo injection experiments in Figure 5E, E', G.

claim: Both activation of endogenous CB1Rs and actomyosin contractility are required for correct pathfinding of corticofugal axons.
source: Together with our above findings showing that activation of endogenous CB1Rs in organotypic slices leads to NM II-dependent arrest or contraction of axonal growth cones, these results suggest that both activation of endogenous CB1Rs and actomyosin contractility are required for correct path finding of corticofugal axons.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of ex vivo and in vivo experimental results.

claim: Treatment with 100 nM WIN results in rapid rounding of Neuro2A cell body and retraction of neurites.
source: Treatment with 100 nM WIN resulted in rapid rounding of the cell body and in retraction of neurites, leaving behind retraction-fiber-like remnants (Figure 6A,B and Video 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 6A, B and Video 6.

claim: F-actin is reorganized and accumulates at the end of the retraction bulb and under the plasma membrane of the cell body after WIN treatment in Neuro2A cells.
source: F-actin was reorganized and accumulated at the end of the retraction bulb and under the plasma membrane of the cell body.
evidence: This is observed in imaging data from Neuro2A cells.

claim: WIN-induced cell rounding in Neuro2A cells can be blocked by blebbistatin treatment.
source: This WIN-induced cell rounding could be blocked by blebbistatin treatment (25 µM) (Figure 6B), suggesting that the observed rapid morphological changes are due to a CB1R-induced general contraction of the actomyosin cell cortex, which is the association of plasma membrane lipids and the underlying actin filament network.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 6B.

claim: Rapid morphological changes in Neuro2A cells are due to CB1R-induced general contraction of the actomyosin cell cortex.
source: This WIN-induced cell rounding could be blocked by blebbistatin treatment (25 µM) (Figure 6B), suggesting that the observed rapid morphological changes are due to a CB1R-induced general contraction of the actomyosin cell cortex, which is the association of plasma membrane lipids and the underlying actin filament network.
evidence: This is inferred from the blockade of morphological changes by blebbistatin.

claim: The stiffness of unstimulated Neuro2A cells is approximately 300 Pa.
source: Averaged AFM measurements in force mode with a 1-µm spherical bead attached to the cantilever (Figure 6C) indicated that the stiffness (Young's modulus) of unstimulated individual cells was approximately 300 Pa, close to values reported in acutely isolated hippocampal glial cells and neurons (Lu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is measured by atomic force microscopy as shown in Figure 6C.

claim: WIN stimulation leads to rapid and transient increase of cell stiffness at different locations on Neuro2A cells.
source: WIN stimulation led to an overall rapid and transient increase of cell stiffness at different locations on the same cell, with the exception of the trailing edge (Figure 6C4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by AFM measurements in Figure 6C.

claim: WIN-induced increase in cell stiffness can be prevented by pre-treatment with blebbistatin.
source: The important transient WIN-induced increase in cell stiffness was absent during incubation with vehicle solution and could be prevented by pre-treatment with blebbistatin (25 µM) (Figure 6D), showing that activation of NM II is necessary to induce the measured changes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by AFM measurements in Figure 6D.

claim: Activation of NM II is necessary to induce WIN-mediated changes in cell stiffness.
source: The important transient WIN-induced increase in cell stiffness was absent during incubation with vehicle solution and could be prevented by pre-treatment with blebbistatin (25 µM) (Figure 6D), showing that activation of NM II is necessary to induce the measured changes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the blockade of stiffness changes by blebbistatin in Figure 6D.

claim: Localized blebbing of the cell membrane occurs starting at early stages (∼2 min) of WIN-induced contraction and ceases after 6-8 min.
source: Moreover, we observed localized blebbing behavior of the cell membrane, starting at the early stages (∼2 min) of the contraction and ceasing after 6–8 min (Figure 6E and Video 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D reconstruction imaging in Figure 6E and Video 7.

claim: CB1R activation leads to rapid and NM II-dependent neurite retraction and rounding of the cell body in Neuro2A cells.
source: In conclusion, our results show that CB1R activation leads to rapid and NM II-dependent neurite retraction and rounding of the cell body in Neuro2A cells, which is accompanied by formation of retraction fibers and by transient increase in cell stiffness and blebbing behavior.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: CB1R activation is accompanied by formation of retraction fibers and transient increase in cell stiffness and blebbing behavior.
source: In conclusion, our results show that CB1R activation leads to rapid and NM II-dependent neurite retraction and rounding of the cell body in Neuro2A cells, which is accompanied by formation of retraction fibers and by transient increase in cell stiffness and blebbing behavior.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the various measurements in Figure 6.

claim: Global CB1R activation results in large-scale contraction of the neuronal cytoskeleton mechanistically similar to mitotic cell rounding.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that global CB1R activation results in large-scale contraction of the neuronal cytoskeleton, which is mechanistically similar to the molecular machinery engaged in mitotic cell rounding.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarities in morphological changes, stiffness increase, and blebbing behavior observed in CB1R-activated neurons and dividing cells.

claim: Chronic in vitro activation of CB1Rs leads to significant inhibition of dendritic development in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: Previously, we have reported that chronic in vitro activation of CB1Rs leads to significant inhibition of dendritic development in cultured hippocampal neurons, while genetic or pharmacological inhibition of CB1Rs leads to more numerous and longer dendrites (Vitalis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors (Vitalis et al., 2008).

claim: Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of CB1Rs leads to more numerous and longer dendrites.
source: Previously, we have reported that chronic in vitro activation of CB1Rs leads to significant inhibition of dendritic development in cultured hippocampal neurons, while genetic or pharmacological inhibition of CB1Rs leads to more numerous and longer dendrites (Vitalis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Vitalis et al., 2008).

claim: Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of CB1R leads to more complex somatodendritic morphology in septal cholinergic neurons.
source: Similarly, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of CB1R leads to more complex somatodendritic morphology in septal cholinergic neurons (Keimpema et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Keimpema et al., 2013.

claim: Increased NM II activity through constitutively active MLCK or RhoA decreases both the length and number of neurites in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: It was reported that increased NM II activity, through constitutively active MLCK or RhoA, decreases both the length and number of neurites and, consequently, delays or abolishes the development of neuronal polarity in cultured hippocampal neurons (Kollins et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kollins et al., 2009.

claim: Neurons expressing CB1R-eCFP, LifeAct-mCherry, and EB3-eGFP at DIV9 respond to 100 nM WIN with rapid morphological reorganization of the somatodendritic compartment.
source: First, we verified the presence of the rapid structural effects of CB1R activation in the somatodendritic region. Neurons expressing CB1R-eCFP, LifeAct-mCherry, and EB3-eGFP at DIV9 responded to 100 nM WIN with rapid morphological reorganization of the somatodendritic compartment, characterized by retraction of distal dendritic regions and broadening of the proximal portion of dendrites (Figure 7A,A' and Video 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging in Figure 7A, A' and Video 8.

claim: WIN-induced somatodendritic reorganization is characterized by retraction of distal dendritic regions and broadening of proximal dendrites.
source: Neurons expressing CB1R-eCFP, LifeAct-mCherry, and EB3-eGFP at DIV9 responded to 100 nM WIN with rapid morphological reorganization of the somatodendritic compartment, characterized by retraction of distal dendritic regions and broadening of the proximal portion of dendrites (Figure 7A,A' and Video 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 7A, A' and Video 8.

claim: Microtubules in individual dendrites display characteristic bent morphology parallel to the appearance of straight cable-like F-actin bundles after WIN treatment.
source: While the overall dynamics of EB3-eGFP comets was not apparently modified, the MTs in individual dendrites often displayed a characteristic bent morphology, parallel to the appearance of straight cable-like F-actin bundles (Figure 7A,A' and Video 8) suggesting the presence of a rapid CB1R-activation-dependent actomyosin contraction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 7A, A' and Video 8.

claim: Overnight treatment with WIN results in a significant decrease in the number of dendrites of developing hippocampal neurons.
source: Overnight treatment with WIN (100 nM) resulted in a significant decrease in the number of dendrites of developing hippocampal neurons, expressing Flag-CB1R-eGFP and the soluble cytoplasmic marker DsRed2 at DIV4 (Figure 7B,C), as reported previously (Vitalis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is demonstrated by morphological analysis in Figure 7B, C.

claim: The effect of WIN on dendrite number is abolished in the presence of Y-27632 or blebbistatin.
source: This effect was abolished in the presence of both Y-27632 (10 µM) or blebbistatin (25 µM) (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 7B, C.

claim: Treatment with ROCK and NM II inhibitors leads to more developed dendrites in control conditions.
source: Notably, treatment with both inhibitors led to more developed dendrites also in control conditions, confirming previous reports on the constitutive inhibition of neurite development through ROCK and NM II (Kollins et al., 2009).
evidence: This is observed in experimental data and supported by citation to Kollins et al., 2009.

claim: Chronic activation of CB1Rs reshapes somatodendritic morphology through enhancement of ROCK- and NM II-mediated contractile tone.
source: In conclusion, our results show that the chronic activation of CB1Rs reshapes somatodendritic morphology through enhancement of the naturally present ROCK- and NM II-mediated contractile tone of neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Acute CB1R activation results in rapid contraction of the neuronal actomyosin cytoskeleton.
source: Our results show that acute CB1R activation results in rapid contraction of the neuronal actomyosin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the Results section.

claim: CB1R acts through heterotrimeric G12/G13 proteins, Rho GTPase, and ROCK to induce contractile interaction of NM II with F-actin.
source: CB1R acts through heterotrimeric G12/G13 proteins, Rho GTPase, and ROCK to induce the contractile interaction of NM II with F-actin.
evidence: This is a summary of the signaling pathway characterized in the study.

claim: CB1R-induced contraction triggers retraction of the actin-rich growth cone of the most distal 60-70 µm of the axon in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: This contraction triggers the retraction of the actin-rich growth cone of the most distal 60–70 µm of the axon in cultured hippocampal neurons and in cortical neurons in organotypic slices.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: CB1R-induced contraction triggers retraction of growth cones in cortical neurons in organotypic slices.
source: This contraction triggers the retraction of the actin-rich growth cone of the most distal 60–70 µm of the axon in cultured hippocampal neurons and in cortical neurons in organotypic slices.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CB1Rs or NM II during brain development leads to excessive growth of corticofugal axons in vivo.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of either CB1Rs or NM II during brain development leads to excessive growth of corticofugal axons in vivo, suggesting that CB1R-induced actomyosin contractility is necessary for the correct pathfinding by mediating their repulsion from the sub-ventricular zone.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo injection experiments in Figure 5.

claim: CB1R-induced actomyosin contractility is necessary for correct pathfinding by mediating repulsion of corticofugal axons from the sub-ventricular zone.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of either CB1Rs or NM II during brain development leads to excessive growth of corticofugal axons in vivo, suggesting that CB1R-induced actomyosin contractility is necessary for the correct pathfinding by mediating their repulsion from the sub-ventricular zone.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vivo experimental results showing that blocking either CB1Rs or NM II leads to axonal invasion of the SVZ.

claim: CB1R-induced actomyosin contraction leads to neurite retraction, cell rounding, and significant elevation in cell rigidity in Neuro2A cells.
source: This contractile behavior is not limited to the growth cone since CB1R-induced actomyosin contraction leads to neurite retraction, cell rounding, and a significant elevation in cell rigidity in the Neuro2A cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: In the somatodendritic region of cultured hippocampal neurons, distal regions of dendrites retract while proximal parts broaden after CB1R activation.
source: Similarly, in the somatodendritic region of cultured hippocampal neurons, distal regions of dendrites retract while proximal parts broaden.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 7A, A'.

claim: ROCK and NM II mediate the inhibitory effect of chronic CB1R activation on dendrite development.
source: Finally, ROCK and NM II mediate the inhibitory effect of chronic CB1R activation on dendrite development, by increasing the natural contractile tone of neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by chronic treatment experiments in Figure 7B, C.

claim: NM II plays a pivotal role in control of tissue architecture through cell reshaping and movement processes.
source: Owing to its position downstream of convergent signaling pathways, the NM II protein plays a pivotal role in the control of tissue architecture through its participation in processes that require cell reshaping and movement, such as cell adhesion, cell migration, and cell division (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In neurons, NM II is involved in neuronal migration and structural organization of the growth cone.
source: In neurons, NM II is also involved in diverse aspects of cell movement, such as neuronal migration and the structural organization and efficient extension of the growth cone, which requires an intricate balance between dynein, microtubules, actin, and different myosin II isoforms (Vallee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Vallee et al., 2009.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition or genetic silencing of NM II leads to disorganization of the growth cone and allows rapid axon extension over inhibitory substrates.
source: Remarkably, previous in vitro results have shown that NM II is important for turning in response to boundaries of substrate-bound laminin-1 (Turney and Bridgman, 2005) and that pharmacological inhibition or genetic silencing of NM II leads to disorganization of the growth cone, allowing rapid axon extension over inhibitory substrates (Hur et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment leads to elevated axonal invasion of the embryonic sub-ventricular zone in vivo.
source: In the present study, we report a comparable in vivo effect, by showing that blebbistatin treatment leads to elevated axonal invasion of the embryonic sub-ventricular zone (SVZ).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo injection experiments in Figure 5.

claim: These results show for the first time the existence of NM II-mediated axonal repulsion in vivo.
source: To our knowledge, these results show for the first time the existence of NM II-mediated axonal repulsion in vivo, suggesting that mobilization of NM II participates in the correct guidance of corticofugal axonal projections.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on the in vivo data.

claim: Mobilization of NM II participates in the correct guidance of corticofugal axonal projections.
source: To our knowledge, these results show for the first time the existence of NM II-mediated axonal repulsion in vivo, suggesting that mobilization of NM II participates in the correct guidance of corticofugal axonal projections.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vivo experimental results.

claim: The endocannabinoid 2-AG is synthesized by DAGLα which is specifically expressed at high levels by proliferating progenitor cells of the SVZ.
source: Since pharmacological CB1R blockade has similar effects to NM II inhibition (i.e., excessive axonal growth), a likely scenario suggests that the endocannabinoid 2-AG, whose synthesizing enzyme DAGLα is specifically expressed at high levels by proliferating progenitor cells of the SVZ (Goncalves et al., 2008), acts through CB1Rs to repulse invading corticofugal axons through NM II-mediated growth cone retraction.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goncalves et al., 2008.

claim: 2-AG acts through CB1Rs to repulse invading corticofugal axons through NM II-mediated growth cone retraction.
source: Since pharmacological CB1R blockade has similar effects to NM II inhibition (i.e., excessive axonal growth), a likely scenario suggests that the endocannabinoid 2-AG, whose synthesizing enzyme DAGLα is specifically expressed at high levels by proliferating progenitor cells of the SVZ (Goncalves et al., 2008), acts through CB1Rs to repulse invading corticofugal axons through NM II-mediated growth cone retraction.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism inferred from the experimental results and prior knowledge.

claim: CB1Rs not only alter the internal organization of the growth cone but cause retraction of the distal axon over several tens of microns.
source: Notably, CB1Rs not only alter the internal organization of the growth cone, as suggested previously (Berghuis et al., 2007; Argaw et al., 2011), but cause the retraction of the distal axon over several tens of microns, both in cultured hippocampal neurons and in cortical neurons in organotypic slices.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: NM II-dependent contraction leads to characteristic periodic bending of microtubules.
source: This NM II-dependent contraction leads to the characteristic periodic bending of microtubules.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2.

claim: Periodic microtubule bending was observed during strong NM II-mediated retraction in DRG neurons after LPA receptor activation.
source: This particular phenotype was similarly observed during strong NM II-mediated retraction in DRG neurons after the activation of the LPA receptor (Bouquet et al., 2007) or after treatment with Sema 3A (Gallo et al., 2002; Wylie and Chantler, 2003; Gallo, 2006;).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Nitric oxide induces similar rapid axonal retraction accompanied by periodic bends.
source: In addition, nitric oxide, widely recognized to induce axonal retractions during development (Cramer et al., 1998; Ernst et al., 2000), was reported to induce similar rapid axonal retraction accompanied by periodic bends (He et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: RhoA, ROCK, and NM II are constitutive inhibitors of neurite development.
source: In addition, RhoA, ROCK, and NM II are known constitutive inhibitors of neurite development (Kollins et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Endo- or exogenous cannabinoids mobilize a myosin-activating machinery involved in growth cone navigation and establishment of neuronal morphology.
source: By activating the CB1R/G12/G13/Rho GTPase/ROCK/NM II axis characterized in our study, endo- or exogenous cannabinoids are likely to mobilize a widely employed myosin-activating machinery that is involved in growth cone navigation and in the establishment and maintenance of neuronal morphology.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental characterization of the signaling pathway.

claim: Similar G12/G13-dependent signaling mechanism is mobilized downstream of LPA receptor and GPR55.
source: Interestingly, similar G12/G13-dependent signaling mechanism is mobilized downstream of at least two developmentally implied neuronal GPCRs, the LPA receptor (Katoh et al., 1998; Kranenburg et al., 1999) and GPR55, a putative 'atypical' cannabinoid receptor (Ryberg et al., 2007; Sharir and Abood, 2010), through activation by lysophosphatidylinositols but not through genuine cannabinoid ligands (Obara et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: NM II is involved in integrin-mediated cell adhesion.
source: NM II is also involved in integrin-mediated cell adhesion; in turn, the adhesive properties of the substrate also control NM II activation (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CB1R-mediated morphological effects may not result from reduced neuronal adhesion considering the time-scale of rapid neuronal retraction.
source: However, CB1R-mediated morphological effects reported in the present study may not result from reduced neuronal adhesion, considering the time-scale of the rapid neuronal retraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the rapid kinetics of the observed effects.

claim: Retracting Neuro2A cells and growth cones leave behind thin membranous fibers that contain F-Actin and are still attached to the adhesive substrate.
source: Instead, retracting the Neuro2A cells and growth cones of hippocampal neurons both in vitro and ex vivo leave behind thin membranous fibers, which contain F-Actin and are still attached to the adhesive substrate.
evidence: This is observed in imaging data from Figures 1, 4, and 6.

claim: The formation and morphology of retraction fibers are similar to those reported in mitotic cells generated by rapid contraction of the cellular actomyosin cortex.
source: The formation and morphology of these fibers are similar to those of retraction fibers reported in mitotic cells (Cramer and Mitchison, 1995) also generated by rapid contraction of the cellular actomyosin cortex (Théry and Bornens, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on mitotic cells.

claim: Endocannabinoids acting through CB1Rs exert a general negative effect on cell spreading and neurite growth.
source: The ensemble of these results combined with the bulk of the available experimental data (reviewed in Gaffuri et al., 2012) suggests that endocannabinoids acting through CB1Rs exert a general negative effect on cell spreading and neurite growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citation to a review.

claim: Basal CB1R activation yields relatively weak tonic inhibition of growth in neuronal sub-regions where F-actin is present.
source: Basal cell-autonomous or paracrine activation of CB1Rs would yield relatively weak tonic inhibition of growth in the majority of developmental settings in all neuronal sub-regions where F-actin is present.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Local growth-promoting effectors may locally surmount weak CB1R-mediated negative tone.
source: Local growth-promoting effectors at the growth cone, such as the self-amplifying autocrine promoter BDNF (Cheng et al., 2011) or netrin-1 (Argaw et al., 2011), may locally surmount this weak negative tone.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Widespread CB1R-mediated weak inhibition helps neurons focus resources to limited growth locations, leading to more efficient polarized growth.
source: The resulting 'channeling' effect of widespread CB1R-mediated weak inhibition would help the neuron to focus its resources to a limited amount of growth locations, leading to more efficient polarized growth.
evidence: This is a proposed functional model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Weak CB1R-mediated inhibition may coordinate guidance of axonal fascicles where moderate eCB production by nearby axons serves as a repulsion cue.
source: Such weak inhibition may serve also to coordinated guidance of axonal fascicles in the brain where moderate production of eCBs by nearby axons would be used as a repulsion cue that helps axons to grow straightly towards their target.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for axonal guidance.

claim: Enhanced eCB signaling in regions highly enriched with eCBs could result in growth cone arrest, repulsion, or collapse.
source: However, when growth cones reach a region highly enriched with eCBs, such as the sub-ventricular zone, enhanced eCB signaling could result in growth cone arrest, repulsion, or collapse, efficiently steering out CB1R-expressing axons from these areas.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by the in vivo experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: CB1R-induced actomyosin contractility may contribute to establish functionally adequate somatodendritic morphology.
source: Finally, CB1R-induced actomyosin contractility may also contribute to establish functionally adequate somatodendritic morphology, acting as a negative regulator of dendritic growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on dendritic development in Figure 7.

claim: The amplitudes of reported cytoskeleton changes are likely dramatic compared to CB1R-induced remodeling in typical physiological settings.
source: In our study, we were able to characterize in detail CB1R-induced actomyosin contraction, which is rather subtle and transitory downstream of endogenous GPCRs, by using high-resolution time-lapse imaging, atomic force microscopy, and moderate over-expression of CB1Rs. Consequently, the amplitudes of reported cytoskeleton changes are likely dramatic compared to CB1R-induced remodeling in typical physiological settings.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of potential limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: Results concerning endogenous CB1Rs obtained in cultured neurons, organotypic slices, and in vivo suggest physiological relevance for the findings.
source: Nevertheless, the results concerning endogenous CB1Rs, obtained in cultured neurons, in organotypic slices, and in vivo suggest physiological relevance for our findings.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from endogenous CB1R experiments in Figures 1H-I, 4C-E, and 5.

claim: NM II-mediated actomyosin contraction conveys a wide-ranging inhibitory role for cannabinoids in neuronal expansion and growth.
source: In conclusion, we identify NM II-mediated actomyosin contraction as a mechanism conveying a wide-ranging inhibitory role for cannabinoids in neuronal expansion and growth, downstream of CB1R coupled to G12/G13 proteins and the Rho-associated kinase ROCK.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Modulation of the neural actomyosin cytoskeleton has not been reported downstream of neurotransmitter GPCRs.
source: Such modulation of the neural actomyosin cytoskeleton has not yet been reported downstream of neurotransmitter GPCRs, therefore our results open previously unexpected perspectives in the study and comprehension of brain function.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.
